blocks.cap: Actor Morag Peacock before the AI mask was applied. Photo Investigation Discovery

blocks.x: Investigation Discovery's (ID) three-part documentary 'Unmasking a Monster: Aileen Wuornos' used an AI mask tool in post-production. It changed actor Morag Peacock's face to exactly match serial killer Wuornos, and did the same for nine other actors, giving them the faces of the real people they played.

Executive producer Steven Dost says this approach is a first for the industry. He calls the technology 'very advanced motion capture.' Showing the face had to have a reason, and what came to mind was Wuornos, whose pain was etched into her face. There is very little documentary footage of Wuornos. ID president Jason Sarlanis said reenactments had always been a barrier to authenticity, and the digital makeup brought a new level of authenticity.

Conventional reenactments deliberately avoid showing the actor's face. This time, the camera looked straight at it. With the technology available, they needed an actor with a similar face shape, and Peacock underwent 90 minutes of makeup and wore a single dental prosthetic. What carried the weight was her eyes. Dost recalled that after a take, 'you could have heard a pin drop.'

Peacock herself hesitated at first. 'Anyone who sees the word AI thinks, wait a minute.' She accepted only after going over with her agent exactly what was being asked of her. 'I wasn't replaced or cloned. It's not creating an AI persona. In the end it's like CGI, and it's still me.' She said that after watching the trailer, she could see her own face beneath the mask.

Dost flatly states that 'the idea that AI speeds up the work is wrong.' Doing it properly actually makes things much slower. It took three years to use AI 'ethically.' Sarlanis said they spent as much time developing usage guidelines as they did on the technology itself. The series premiered on ID and HBO Max.

blocks.cap: Photo Utopai

blocks.x: Utopai Studio has released PAI, a system for film and TV production, along with Utopai X, a video generation model. PAI combines video generation, production context, and a filmmaker-centered workflow in one place.

Having been developed inside a working studio, it was built to fit the demands of a professional production environment. It plans shots, creates assets, generates footage, reviews takes, and manages revisions. Throughout, the script, characters, locations, assets, and creative decisions remain continuously connected.

Utopai X is PAI's video generation layer. According to the company, it ranks second in the world on Artificial Analysis's 'text-to-video with audio' leaderboard, with an Elo score of 1,150. It trails first place by 9 points and ranks highest among US company models. The ranking is determined by blind preference tests in which participants compare outputs without knowing which model produced them.

Utopai X excels at difficult visual effects like reflections and caustics, world understanding, and spatial consistency. It helps keep continuity and the environment stable even as shots become more complex.

When a script is fed into PAI, it is organized by scene and shot. Characters, locations, objects, visual references, and production decisions are all tied to the project. Utopai's AI agent, the 'Production Assistant,' reads this context and helps with shot planning, ideas, and new versions. What to create, keep, or revise is decided by the filmmaker.

Within PAI, shots can be assembled and footage pulled from Utopai X, with multiple takes compared side by side. Earlier versions remain intact, and the chosen footage moves on to existing editing and post-production pipelines like Adobe Premiere and DaVinci Resolve. Utopai is already using both tools on its own productions, including the animated feature 'The Most Serious Part,' written and directed by Mike Bender.

blocks.cap: Trailer for the short film 'Paradise Lost - Universe.' Courtesy of CJ ENM

blocks.x: 'Paradise Lost - Universe,' a short film series that expands the world of director Yeon Sang-ho's new movie 'Paradise Lost,' is being released.

Distributor CJ ENM announced on the 28th that it would post the first installment, 'Your Seaweed Soup,' and the second, 'You Have Dad,' on the 29th on YouTube, Naver TV, Instagram, Facebook and other platforms.

'Paradise Lost - Universe' is a prequel set in the same world as the film 'Paradise Lost.' It weaves together episodes about different people living in an era when artificial intelligence (AI) technology that lets you meet departed loved ones again has become part of everyday life.

Episode 1, 'Your Seaweed Soup,' follows an elderly man who lost his wife and sits across from her again through an unfamiliar device. Episode 2, 'You Have Dad,' depicts the strange story of a young girl who lost her father reuniting with him as recreated inside an unfamiliar pair of glasses.
It was made using generative AI, based on a script written by director Yeon Sang-ho. The music was composed by Chae Min-ju, who also scored 'Paradise Lost.'

The film 'Paradise Lost' follows Ryu So-young (played by Kim Hyun-joo), a mother whose son went missing in an accident, as she reunites with her son Ryu Seon-woo (Bae Hyun-sung) after nine years. Ryu So-young had been enduring her grief by relying on 'trans-human' technology that recreates her dead son using AI.

blocks.cap: Greta Garbo in 'Anna Christie,' 1930. Photo MGM/Sportsphoto/Allstar

blocks.x: Greta Garbo, who lit up the silent film era and even its first talkie, may appear in a film of the AI age. It has been more than 100 years since her screen debut, and decades since her remains were buried in a forest cemetery in Sweden. Her descendants have signaled they would consider having an AI Garbo take on a 21st-century film role.

Garbo's likeness has already been revived with AI in an ad for the Swedish industrial company SKF. The technique, which critics call 'ghostsploitation,' was also used for Val Kilmer, who died last year. Craig Ryskamp, one of three relatives managing her estate, left open the possibility of a film role, saying 'I wouldn't say no.' There's also a connection in that Garbo's second screen appearance was a 1921 promotional film featuring SKF.
In the 99-second ad, the AI Garbo's performance is cross-cut with footage of ball bearings. Ryskamp said he was 'completely blown away' by how it captured her gestures, costume, face and even voice.

The production team created Garbo using China's Seedream and Google's Nano Banana Pro, among other tools. Because of copyright, no footage or photos of Garbo were fed into the AI. Instead, features like her ice-blue eyes and wavy blonde bob were described through text prompts. A real actor performed, and an AI-generated likeness was layered on top. Her voice was recreated from early film recordings.

The result appears to move past the 'uncanny valley.' The dialogue doesn't quite reach the level of MGM's writers. Ryskamp said that whoever holds the rights to Garbo's voice, name and image is 'very particular' about choosing partners. Her likeness has been used by Ferragamo, Gucci and Louis Vuitton before, but this is the first time in moving footage. The ad ends with the famous 'Grand Hotel' line, 'I want to be alone.'

blocks.cap: Artwork for 'Storm Dogs'

blocks.x: Rob Minkoff, who co-directed Disney's 'The Lion King' and made 'Stuart Little', is in final talks to join the AI-driven film 'Storm Dogs'. It is the next project from Particle6, the studio behind Tilly Norwood.
It is a family comedy-drama. A storm hits a rural English village, and a baby named Poppy, separated from her guardian, teams up with a pack of dogs to find her way home.
Minkoff will serve as creative lead, working with van der Velden on the story, characters and script. The project is still in development, with filming targeted to start in 2027.

“Rob is someone who has created animal characters that have stayed with film history. His understanding of character, comedy and emotionally grounded storytelling makes him a special creative partner for 'Storm Dogs'.” That is what van der Velden said in a statement.

Minkoff added his own comment. “Much of my career has been spent finding ways to make animal characters that are funny, emotionally true and fully alive. When I visited Particle6 in London, I met filmmakers who care deeply about story, character and performance. They are also seriously exploring how far a new production method can carry a director's imagination onto the screen.”

According to Particle6, the film pairs live-action performance with photorealistic animated characters. It blends AI tools, traditional methods and real actors. The process does not just capture an actor's voice, but transfers facial expression, gesture and intonation onto the animated character.

The baby and the dogs are 'created' through a mix of live-action performance and AI. A company spokesperson called bringing Poppy and the dogs to life with AI a 'real bonus', since neither a baby nor animals need to stay on set for long stretches. Van der Velden said the nature of the film itself is 'an extremely difficult challenge with conventional production methods alone'.

“Bringing together performers, filmmakers and brand-new tools lets us attempt something unusually ambitious while keeping every creative decision in human hands.” He added, “We have no interest in AI replacing human creativity. But we do see enormous potential for it to change how films get made.” Van der Velden noted that this shift is still at a pioneering stage.

Development of 'Storm Dogs' comes a few months after Particle6 cast Tilly Norwood as the lead of its first feature, 'Misaligned'. 'Misaligned' began filming this month. Last week, Tilly Norwood was put in front of outlets including Variety and 'Good Morning Britain', and during an interview with Piers Morgan, she abruptly switched from English to Cantonese.

blocks.cap: 'A Woman Asleep'

blocks.x: Turkish art-house distributor Baska Sinema has bought the domestic theatrical distribution rights to 'A Woman Asleep'. It is an experimental AI feature made in English, directed by artist and filmmaker Viki Bardo.

Bardo is regarded as one of the early artists working with photo-based AI art and video art. In 2023 she gave a TEDx talk on AI and art. Her work has been shown in New York, Paris, London, Berlin, Rome and Miami, among other cities. Her AI short 'Dreamt by Another' screened at more than 40 film festivals, and MUBI recently secured its Turkish rights.

'A Woman Asleep' takes as its starting point the 1974 French cult film 'The Man Who Sleeps'. That film was co-directed by Bernard Queysanne and Georges Perec, and it was itself an adaptation of Perec's novel 'A Man Asleep'.

It is an 80-minute AI drama. Its synopsis describes it as looking at alienation and numbness in a hyper-connected age. It will open in spring 2027 through Baska Sinema in 20 Turkish cities, an unusual path for an AI feature.

Production was handled by Spongewash, a Turkish AI production studio. It made the AI documentary 'Post Truth', directed by Alkan Avcıoğlu, which drew attention on the festival circuit, and that film also reached Turkish theaters through Baska Sinema.

The narration was delivered by an AI voice clone trained on the director's own voice. Promotional material explains it this way: “This choice extends the film's conceptual framework and dreamlike quality, letting the narration exist in a space between the human and the synthetic. It also fits the world the film portrays.” It cites the narrative approaches of Alain Resnais, Michelangelo Antonioni, Chris Marker and Apichatpong Weerasethakul as references.
The film was edited from a pool of 50,000 cuts. It took two years to complete.

“I spent five years focused on making AI films, before the topic had even become popular in the film world.” That is what Bardo said in a statement. “The most interesting use of AI is not to reproduce Hollywood's forms. It lies in giving the freedom to make personal, formally ambitious films that would be hard to fund unless you are an independent filmmaker.”

Baska Sinema CEO Armaan Lale said, “Our interest is not in the technology itself, but in how far filmmakers can expand the expressive possibilities of film with new tools.” He added, “'A Woman Asleep' looks at a society shaped by technological dependence and emotional disconnection through a distinctive, woman-centered perspective. What matters to us is whether these tools are used in service of a clear cinematic vision.”

Runway walked through, from start to finish, how it made the 'Game of Horse' video. The most common comment, they said, was 'Wait, is this AI? How did they make it?' Host Ian confirms everything was made in Runway and goes through the techniques used, in order.

The first step is the story. 'Game of Horse' uses a call-and-response, cause-and-effect structure as is: a finger snap triggers something strange, and the other person has to handle it. If they can't, they lose a point.

They also offered five rules to follow when building a different story: give a character the audience will care about a clear desire and something to lose, place obstacles in their way, show instead of explain, end somewhere different from where you started, and cut anything that doesn't serve the desire, the obstacle, or the change.

Character development moves quickly with the Runway agent. You just specify the type of character and how many variations you want, and if you plan to make a character sheet afterward, it's better to generate it against a solid-color background. Ian iterates with Nano Banana 2 Lite, which renders fast, and finishes the images he likes with GPT2 or Nano Banana Pro.

A character sheet is a single image containing a full-body front view, a full-body back view, and a close-up of the face. It matters because it lets you pass a lot of context to omni-style models in one image. One is made for each major character.

For costumes, you feed in the character sheet with a prompt to change the outfit. If there's a reference clothing image, it goes in too. They used Muse Image, which preserves identity well and generates fast. Locations follow the same process, except they describe a space instead of a person.

They named the burst method as a way to keep scene continuity. Continuity is handled with a video model instead of an image model. In tool mode, you pick SeeDance 2.5, upload the character sheet and location reference, then sketch out rough blocking with the annotation feature and run it at 1080p for five seconds. One five-second generation replaces many rounds of image iteration and costs fewer credits. Because everything is generated together in the same moment, scene continuity is essentially guaranteed. From there, pulling out the frames you like gives you the coverage you need.

Character voices are made by taking a scene image pulled from the burst as the starting frame and having the character say a short line toward the camera with no music. That voice is either used as is or refined by swapping it into another model.

The video description links to a Claude skill Ian built. It reads an input image and a short idea, then turns them into a prompt dense enough to drop straight into Runway's SeeDance 2.5. Using the Runway MCP lets you generate the video right inside a Claude session. Ask for several variations and it produces different versions with camera angles that don't overlap.

The editing advice is simple: keep only the generated parts with good flow and drop anything that looks off, then add music and place the tension and the laughs. The prompts used and the Claude skill are available at runway.com/prompts/a-game-of-horse.

blocks.cap: Inferstudio's 'Daughter of the Inner Stars'

blocks.x: 'Daughter of the Inner Stars' is a 50-minute animated orchestral film performance. It was designed to introduce children to symphonic music, weaving original animation into live narration and orchestral performance. The production grew far larger in scale as it came together.

The team grounded the work in hand-made assets, traditional storyboards and real actors, then used Autodesk Flow Studio's AI motion-capture workflow, which turns reference footage into editable 3D character animation. What emerged was something the team had not imagined at first.

It premiered in 2024 at the Sydney Opera House with the Sydney Symphony Orchestra, then came to North America in 2025 with the Vancouver Symphony Orchestra. The story follows a girl named Pia searching for her lost father amid a war among the stars.

Composer Nicholas Buc, writer-director James Vinson and producer Melanie Hiluta first imagined something closer to a picture book on stage: characters drawn by Ukraine's Tuvik Studio shown as still 2D images while a narrator carried the story.

The move to 3D began when production designer Nathan Su, a former architect who founded Inferstudio, joined the project. Eighteen months before the premiere, the arrival of Flow Studio and Unreal Engine's MetaHuman Animator opened a path to animating the characters as well.

blocks.cap: An actor's motion capture and the 3D character render

blocks.x: Flow Studio is a web-based tool that turns live-action performance into 3D character animation without a suit. Upload footage and a 3D character, and AI-assisted motion capture transfers the actor's movement onto the character, previewed within the original scene before the data is exported for further refinement.

In early tests in 2023, character artist Ludvig Holmen filmed a simple motion on his phone and uploaded it. Pia's face and hair were not yet finished, but Flow Studio translated Holmen's performance into Pia's movement with surprising accuracy — an early sign that a full-length animation was possible.

blocks.cap: A scene from the finished animation

blocks.x: The team estimates Flow Studio cut animation time by 80 percent. Using real performances also kept the production from losing its analog feel. The team prioritized emotional resonance over technical perfection.

blocks.cap: Dan Hartley, Julia Stuart, Chris Bird

blocks.x: CineMe, an AI platform for filmmakers and content creators, opens on October 1, 2026. It was founded by Dan Hartley, a BAFTA- and Emmy-nominated director, and Chris Bird, former managing director of Amazon Prime Video UK.

The founders said Julia Stuart has joined CineMe's advisory board. She was formerly director of original films at Sky and now leads international film strategy at STUDIO TF1. In October 2024, The Hollywood Reporter named her among the 'Most Powerful Women in International Television.'

CineMe turns scripts into realistic images and footage, and carries the process through budgeting, scheduling and fundraising in a single collaborative space. It produces storyboards, previsualization and pitch decks meant to attract investment, secure actors and align creative and production teams. Pricing is split into subscription tiers.

"CineMe turns words into worlds, so any storyteller can see, refine, cost, sell and produce," Hartley said. "Anyone with a story should be able to use production-grade tools in one collaborative hub. We want to let people prototype a film at very low cost, raising creative ambition while lowering financial risk."
Co-founder Bird said, "YouTube gave everyone a platform, and Netflix gave everyone a theater. CineMe gives everyone a studio."

Stuart added, "Over the past year, I've watched CineMe come to life alongside Dan. It's a project close to my heart, and I've been involved at every stage, both practical and creative. We set the bar at the highest level, and getting there has been rigorous, at times close to perfectionism. What excites me most is how far technology can push creativity."

In the coming months, Hartley and Bird will set up the 'CineMe 5% Fund,' fulfilling a founding pledge to place 5% of the company's equity into a charitable trust. The goal is to put enterprise-grade AI into the hands of people working in the film industry.

"The pandemic and the strikes pushed a generation of freelancers to the economic brink, and I was one of them," Hartley said. "This is a turning point. The UK can remain the world's leading production hub and set the standard for how this technology is used, but we also need to build the pathways that train today's and tomorrow's workforce."

blocks.cap: 'Wonka's Golden Ticket' (Netflix)

blocks.x: Netflix's competition series 'Wonka's Golden Ticket' loosely adapts Roald Dahl's Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. It's hosted not by a person or an anonymous narrator but by the voice of Gene Wilder, who played Wonka in the 1971 film Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory and died in 2016 at age 83; the voice was recreated with AI.

Variety TV critic Alison Herman places the show alongside 'Squid Game: The Challenge' from about three years ago, calling both rushed reality spin-offs built to turn in-house IP into franchises, ones that misread and distort their source material. Both originals were stories about how it's wrong to push people, especially children, into competing over scarce resources.

The producers state in a disclaimer that they obtained permission from Wilder's estate. Herman writes that even if it's legally fine, questions remain: whether it was necessary, and whether what's gained from using a dead man's voice in a game show outweighs viewers' discomfort.

Netflix acquired the Roald Dahl Story Company in 2021. While drama series based on Dahl's short stories are in development, this show keeps Dahl's work in the conversation, Herman writes, though not for the right reasons.

She found the production design impressive, reviving iconic sets like the chocolate river and the Wonkavision studio. But there are several jarring collisions between old and new beyond the AI Wilder, such as a 1950s-style challenge-intro reel or a 'Love Island'-style shared dormitory.
Contestants pair up for physical challenges and a social game to choose who gets eliminated. The winning prize is $3 million.
Still, the most striking element is Wilder's voice, especially eerie when it cracks jokes. Herman writes that the computer can mimic Wilder's timbre but hasn't (yet) learned comedy's timing.
The first seven episodes are out on Netflix, and the two-part finale airs September 30.

blocks.cap: Retouch4me Lab Video

blocks.x: Retouch4me has released a new AI plugin, Retouch4me Lab Video. The company says it automatically corrects a video's color and applies a cinematic, film-like style.
It runs directly inside editors that support DaVinci Resolve 18 or later and OFX. The company says, "say goodbye to tedious manual base grading."

Digital cameras can be flawlessly sharp, but that can strip a scene of its "soul." Turning ordinary footage into something cinematic can take hours of complex color grading and hunting for the right LUT. Retouch4me says the tool "handles all the heavy technical work, leaving only the pure creativity that matters most."

blocks.cap: An example of Lab Video applied

blocks.x: Lab Video is an AI-based OFX plugin that turns digital footage into a film aesthetic. The company says that whether for wedding videographers, YouTubers or ad production houses, it analyzes every frame and applies color science, film grain and optical effects on the spot to strip away digital's characteristic "sterile" look.

It works differently from a fixed LUT. "The AI analyzes the footage and automatically produces a harmonious, professional-grade grade," the company says. It cites an organic film look built from grain and soft optical distortion, greatly reduced post-production time, and a style that holds up across different lighting and projects.

It adds film grain and subtle optical imperfections to remove digital dryness. It works inside Resolve 18 or later and OFX hosts without needing to export to another program, and can serve either as a final styling tool or as a base for further grading.

It supports Windows 7, 10, 11 or later, and macOS 10.15 or later. On macOS, it only works with the version of DaVinci Resolve downloaded from the official website; the App Store version does not support OFX plugins.
It's a perpetual license with free updates. All processing happens on the user's computer, with no cloud and no subscription. A trial is available on the company's website.

blocks.cap: AI film 'Guardian Monk: Save the World Heritage'

blocks.x: The AI film 'Guardian Monk: Save the World Heritage' will get a special screening in 4DX theaters. Made by generative-AI content studio Mooam (CEO and director Hyun Hae-ri), it opens to audiences on September 27 at CGV Yongsan I'Park Mall, Wangsimni and Centum City's 4DX auditoriums.

It's a Full AI film made from the planning stage with 4DX screening in mind. Centered on a story about protecting world cultural heritage, it ties 4DX-specific effects like motion chairs and environmental effects into the visual direction to suit theatrical viewing.

The planning went beyond simply making footage with AI to consider the screening environment itself. With physical effects added to match each scene, audiences experience the film's story more viscerally.

Production used an AI film production pipeline that Mooam has developed and refined in-house. The AI artists involved are interns Mooam itself incubated, making this a case of in-house-trained AI talent producing content that actually reaches theaters, a real-world application of the production system.

Mooam plans to broaden the formats of its AI film content, including 'Guardian Monk,' and expand its original IP lineup. 'Zenfluencer' received an official invitation to the Rendez-Vous section of France's Canneseries international festival last April and is headed for a theatrical release later this year. A follow-up feature, 'No Transformation Zone,' is also in production.
Going forward, the company plans to keep producing content with its own IP for release across multiple media platforms, including theaters, TV and OTT.

blocks.cap: Zurich Summit AI panel. From left: Natalia Ramos Ahn, Nick Shumaker, Jack London, Nick Holt, Vania Schlögel

blocks.x: At the Zurich Summit this weekend, ‘Musk’ producer Nick Shumaker, Hollywood film investor Vania Schlögel, Jack London, director of ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts,’ and Nick Holt, director of ‘AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About,’ took the stage to discuss the changes AI will bring to film.

Schlögel is the founder and managing partner of LA-based investment firm Atwater Capital. This summer, she became chief strategy officer (CSO) of Magnific, the AI creative platform that rebranded from Freepik. She said she decided to get directly involved after seeing sexualized images of children’s IP, demeaning content toward women, and racist content spreading on rival platforms.

She also voiced concern that the confident tone of AI assistants leads people into ‘cognitive surrender.’ Still, her conclusion was clear: ‘Whether we like it or not, AI is changing society and even how humans empathize. That’s why it matters to be in the driver’s seat.’

Shumaker took a different tack. While acknowledging that AI is a useful tool across the film industry, he raised the issue of generative AI training on original works. ‘Fair use has to be addressed. Taking material without permission to train on is inappropriate.’ He explained that ‘Musk’ itself used almost no AI in production, with AI added only in the lip-sync post-production work on a human-made CGI avatar of Musk.

London, known on YouTube as ‘Gossip Goblin,’ is preparing for the theatrical release of ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts,’ an SF anthology made entirely with AI. He said the polarized debate over AI isn’t very useful, adding, ‘Just as the Luddites didn’t win, the anti-AI movement probably won’t win either.’ Without AI, he explained, the film would have been ‘too obscure and niche’ to get made at all.

Holt, who came to the Zurich Film Festival with a documentary featuring interviews with Geoffrey Hinton and Demis Hassabis, among others, said that for now, AI tools are lowering the barrier to filmmaking.
fxguide released a video showing how to combine Gaussian splats, generative video models, and traditional 3D exports in a single pipeline, with a focus on lighting, FX, and overall creative control.
The title says it all: you don't have to build everything in 3D. In a hybrid setup that mixes 3D and 2D, splats help with the lighting work.

OpenAI Astra is a model that operates a computer directly, handling multi-step tasks on its own. Unlike a video generator, it works with files and apps. Curious Refuge handed it the kind of work an editor or assistant editor would normally do.

The first task was organizing 64 raw clips from a recent shoot. In about 17 minutes and $5, Astra returned the whole project organized, producing a file manifest, an audio-video matching document, a contact sheet, a website for searching footage, and a document explaining the structure — most of which no one had asked for.

blocks.cap: The file manifest Astra created

blocks.x: It didn't sort by metadata alone. It read what was happening inside each clip and labeled it using editor language, like 'intense conversation, reverse OTS.' It also left a command file to revert everything to the original folder structure if the results weren't liked.

The second task was much harder. After handing over footage, screen recordings, and supporting material, and explaining the edit direction via a Loom video, Astra produced a roughly seven-minute YouTube tutorial. It studied the channel on its own and matched its existing design language, down to the green-and-yellow borders. It also delivered an editable Adobe Premiere Pro project, along with a thumbnail, title, description, and chapter markers.

blocks.cap: The Premiere Pro project Astra created

blocks.x: Where creative judgment was needed, the limits showed. The finished cut had problems throughout — pacing, color, audio, and overall polish. The job took one hour and twenty minutes and about $60, and needed enough fixing that the team concluded a human editor is still better for now.

For repetitive work — ingest, logging, renaming clips, audio matching, and project organization — it held up well. The team read this as a sign that an editor's job is shifting from working inside the software by hand to directing the work instead.

Zelda Williams has appealed to fans to stop circulating AI videos of her late father, Robin Williams. It comes nearly a year after she first posted on SNS asking people not to send her AI videos imitating her father.

Williams, who directed ‘Lisa Frankenstein,’ posted on X on Monday. The so-called ‘private videos’ circulating, she said, are ‘obviously AI, and not even good AI.’ ‘If you’re a fan and you believe this, you must have watched his movies on mute. The voice sounds robotic and terrible. But since a person told a robot to make it, I’m talking to you people. Don’t drag him into your delusions — let him rest.’
She added, ‘Just because he’s gone doesn’t mean he’s your puppet. Shame on you.’

Robin Williams, beloved for ‘Jumanji,’ ‘Good Will Hunting,’ ‘Dead Poets Society,’ ‘Hook’ and ‘Mrs. Doubtfire,’ died in 2014 at age 63. In recent years, his likeness has become a frequent target of AI recreations.

This isn’t the first time Zelda has spoken out about AI. In October 2025, she wrote on Instagram, ‘Please stop sending me AI videos of my dad.’ ‘It’s dumb, it’s a waste of time and energy, and trust me, it’s the last thing he’d want.’
Last month, she and her brothers Zak and Cody revived their father’s Instagram account, aiming to push back against the rampant AI misuse of his voice and image.

blocks.cap: Pingyao International Film Festival

blocks.x: Once the 10th Pingyao International Film Festival wraps on September 30, Jia Zhangke will move into location scouting and production design for his next film, the road movie 'Mama Dunhuang.'
Zhao Tao, who won the David di Donatello Award for Best Actress for 'Shun Li and the Poet,' takes the lead again, playing a woman who has stayed at home and sets out on a journey with AI's help.
'We won't use AI to make Mama Dunhuang. AI only plays a role inside the story,' Jia Zhangke said.

At its 5th edition, Pingyao held the 'AI-IF' project with artist Xu Bing, letting audiences make films with AI. But all of the festival's AI projects have been exhibitions, and none of this year's official selections were AI-made. 'We've been cautious. Still, we want to stay open to AI, to watch and embrace it. We shouldn't avoid it — we should understand it and discuss it.' He also made an AI-generated video himself earlier this year.

The festival's operations also came up. This year's official lineup was kept small at 51 films, and visits to the online ticketing system topped 70 million. There is also discussion of building an additional theater seating 300 to 500 inside the ancient walled city, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Unknown Pleasures, the art-house distributor he co-founded, is negotiating to acquire two films that screened at Cannes.
Kling 4.0 arrives this October. The lightweight version, Kling 4.0 Flash, is available now to Ultra annual subscribers.
Kling says this version raises video generation a step further in realism, creative control, and narrative completeness.

Audio and visuals were reworked first. Camera shake is reduced even during large movements, stereo sound quality has improved, and lip sync is more accurate. Resolution reaches up to 4K, with output supporting up to 10-bit HDR.
Omni Reference has also been expanded. Up to 15 multimodal references can now be used, making results more consistent, and video editing features have been strengthened.
The update also focuses on keeping stories uninterrupted. Up to 10 keyframes can be set, and a 30-second video can be generated natively in one go.
A video extension feature has been added, and multiple languages, accents, and dialects are supported. The video closes with the line: "The stage is set. You call the shots."

Theoretically Media rounded up a week of AI news. On the same day, Anthropic released Opus 5.5, and OpenAI released GPT-6 Sol and Luna. Meta expanded Muse into hardware at Meta Connect. After news that Muse overtook ChatGPT in the App Store, Meta also unveiled $1,299 Meta VR glasses, new Ray-Ban Meta glasses, and a separate 5G-equipped "AI Tamagotchi" called Muse Charm. In the host's view, the fight is really about who becomes "your AI best friend."

Video news continued. Alibaba will release a new video model in November. It comes with the usual promises of being longer, more consistent, easier to control, and "smarter," but footage secretly filmed on a phone already looks Seedance-level. Kling 4.0 also resurfaced, reportedly with a refreshed Omni model and a much longer generation length. Traces of Nano Banana 2.5 Flash were found in Google Flow.

Real-time world models were also covered. Odyssey's Agora-2 places up to 20 humans and AI agents together inside an AI-simulated Diablo II world. Pixverse R2 lets users type prompts inside a living world and talk to characters within it. The host called it the closest thing to a holodeck, minus the hologram.

The segment closed with audio news. Seed Audio 1.5 is coming to Pippit, and audio was exactly what Seedance needed most. Fish Audio's Drama 3 preview, billed as "the most controllable TTS model yet," is already on the model list. jam_bot, built by Jordan Rudess and the MIT Media Lab to improvise like Rudess himself, will give a live performance at MIT on October 3.

blocks.cap: Art of the Frame Podcast – Alan Smithee Roundtable

blocks.x: Hosts Scott Simmons, Katie Hinsen, and Michael Kammes discuss the major technological and economic shifts now reshaping film and TV production. The forces driving the change are AI tools, post-production software that is consolidating into unified platforms, and shifting distribution methods. AI acts like a smart assistant inside platforms such as DaVinci Resolve or Adobe Creative Cloud, automatically handling tedious repetitive tasks and understanding natural-language commands, freeing creators to focus on higher-level work. So how much easier does this make direct-to-consumer (D2C) digital releases?

Vertical micro-dramas have also emerged as a new frontier, both creatively and financially. Unlike the failed Quibi, this format relies on fast-paced storytelling and high retention. It has its own storytelling grammar, short production timelines, and modest budgets. Its core audience tends to be viewers the traditional video industry has long overlooked, such as older women who are fans of soap operas. Accessible camera gear, simplified editing, and AI-assisted visual effects have lowered the barrier to entry. Filmmakers and actors are stepping out as independent producers who own their own IP, and a new language of digital storytelling is being created.
Guests Casey Esser and Vanessa von Schwartz share their firsthand experience making vertical micro-dramas, along with a few pieces of news post-production professionals will welcome.

In the 'One Cool Thing' segment, Katie featured VFX editor Corinne Pickett, who set up a workspace on a boat to do VFX and online editing. Michael picked the YouTube channel 'Alan Smithee – Resolve Studio,' which covers scripting and workflow extensions, and Scott picked a New York Times article about the film 'Odyssey' being shot on actual film.

blocks.cap: 'Dear Upstairs Neighbors' poster (courtesy of the production team)

blocks.x: Connie He, a Pixar alum, directed the six-minute short animation 'Dear Upstairs Neighbors,' which first premiered at Sundance in January. It held its world premiere at the Tribeca Festival in June and went on to SIGGRAPH in July. The protagonist, Ada, can't sleep because of noise from her upstairs neighbors. The racket conjures hallucinations that start out beautiful but grow increasingly chaotic, overwhelming her exhausted mind.

The film was produced by Google DeepMind. Connie He and producer Marcie Mayer worked with DeepMind researchers and engineers, and the executive producers are Doug Eck, Glen Entis, and David Salesin. The film's look came from custom versions of Google's Veo and Imagen, fine-tuned on the film's concept art.

blocks.cap: Ada before nightfall (courtesy of the production team)

blocks.x: It began with real insomnia she experienced during the pandemic. "It always started as a personal expression. I never thought it would become an actual short film," she said. She wrote down her feelings on paper at cafes, sketching about 80% of the storyboard, then set it aside for a long time. Later, talking with old Pixar friends about what machine learning might mean for artists, this nearly-finished story became the testing ground. Ada's bedroom recreates the real home of production designer Yingzhong Shin. The rage scenes were shaped by the director's memories of Jackson Pollock, drawn from growing up alongside a father who painted abstracts. Both predate the arrival of generative tools.

The team treated the model not as a button to press but as an instrument to tune. They fine-tuned it on roughly a dozen layered concept art pieces, amounting to hundreds of images. The model picked up a low two-point perspective angle that no one had told it was a rule, and even learned the zigzag lines and brushstrokes drawn wherever objects touched the ground. "We were like, wow, it's picking up on patterns we never even thought about. It was kind of an 'aha' moment," she said.

blocks.cap: One of the hallucinations, the drill (courtesy of the production team)

blocks.x: For fixing shots, the team built a separate 'local correction' tool that adjusts only specific regions of the frame. It wasn't unfamiliar to the director, who worked on 'Inside Out 2' at Pixar and handled Nuke as a CG generalist on Season 1 of 'Love, Death + Robots.' The way of thinking is the same, she said — only the coat has changed. The comedy timing had already been locked in long before generative tools entered the picture, through 27 revisions of the storyboard over a year and a half.

At first, artists and researchers simply spoke different languages. After a hackathon where they tried making a film together with current tools in just a few hours, the researchers quickly realized this approach wouldn't produce a good film. Asked about Hisko Hulsing's 'Danse Macabre' being walked out on and booed at Annecy in June for using generative tools, the director didn't dodge the question. She said there's a huge gap between what the technology actually is and what people think it is. "The way we did it is just one possible approach. Still, that conversation needs to happen first."

blocks.cap: The night gets worse before it gets better (courtesy of the production team)
Image from 'Call of the Wild' (Simon Rumley/nmatic)

blocks.x: David Barron, the British film producer credited on six 'Harry Potter' films, is moving into generative AI. (Deadline exclusive)

Barron has set out to produce an AI-adapted film of Jack London's 1903 novel 'The Call of the Wild.' Simon Rumley ('Crushed,' 'Red White & Blue') will write and direct. The film will be generated at nmatic, with CGI and traditional VFX used together for complex scenes. Because the approach follows the subjective experience of the lead dog, Buck, the filmmakers are positioning it as the first faithful adaptation of the novel.

Barron said: "The canvas London painted is so vast, the Alaskan terrain so brutal, and the dog-and-wolf fights so visceral that a faithful film adaptation has, until now, been impossible both physically and financially. Only now has technology caught up with London's vision, and I believe now is the moment to finally do the novel justice."

The novel follows a St. Bernard raised in comfort in California's Santa Clara Valley who is sold into the brutal world of the 1890s Klondike Gold Rush, discovering the wild instinct that had always lain within him. It has been adapted into film multiple times, including a 2020 version written by Michael Green and starring Harrison Ford.
The film is produced by David Barron, Mark Sandell ('A Liar's Autobiography'), and Nick Price. At nmatic, Chris Catchpole, Karl Little, and Toby White lead the prompting and technical work.

Don Quixote is a novel that has stopped filmmakers in their tracks more than once; Terry Gilliam's repeated, abandoned attempts to adapt it are the most famous case. Animators Guillermo Miranda and Javier de la Chica took another run at it, using AI as their main production tool. The result is a comic adventure about the windmill episode, La Triste Figura (The Sad Figure). It was co-produced by Magnific and first screened in Madrid on September 23.

The audience reaction was unexpected. The AI short landed better with comedy and dialogue than with the action and style it had always been confident about. The writer called it warmer and more human than typical “AI animation.”

blocks.cap: From left: Magnific's Angela Saria, directors Javier de la Chica and Guillermo Miranda

blocks.x: The way they worked was different from the start. Unlike traditional animation, which is split by department, a team of a dozen or so people, sometimes growing to as many as 30, moved freely across stages. The two directors logged into the same project from different cities and watched each other's generations in real time. De la Chica says he wants to turn AI production into a “multiplayer game.”

They didn't just type prompts. They first built turnarounds, expression sheets, and costume tests, and used those as references to generate footage, mostly with Seedance 2.5. Characters and assets were made with Seedream 5 Pro. The final edit, about 120 shots, involved roughly 1,200 generations. The storyboards were hand-drawn by Victor Ponce, and voice actors handled the dialogue.

The limits were just as clear. Miranda calls the result “not the same thing” as animation and refers to the film as a prototype. The hardest part was a roughly five-minute dialogue scene among four characters in front of the windmill. Keeping character consistency was difficult, and because the windmill wouldn't spin steadily without warping, they gave up on physical realism there. Small fixes were hard while whole new sequences came easily, so solving their biggest problem added about one minute and thirty seconds to the running time.

They didn't hide their anxieties either. Some friends in the industry are offended; others are curious but afraid to say so. De la Chica expects hiring to shrink at studios with hundreds of employees. In Miranda's words: “We're a bit in the fog.”
Runway has introduced an “agent tagging” feature. Users can tag the Runway agent wherever an asset lives to call it in.
Once tagged, you can ask it to make an edit, show an alternative, or fix a problem. Runway says it's “that simple.”

The 1-minute-34-second intro video follows a family running the tropical fish shop Wong's Exotic Aquarium in Sunset Park, Brooklyn. When they need an ad for customers, granddaughter Iris reaches for the Runway agent.
The feature is available to try at app.runway.com.

‘The Gifted,’ an AI-made short film, won the first Future Vision XPRIZE, hosted jointly by Google, XPRIZE and Range Media. The contest selects film projects about how technology could change the future.

Directed by Jeff Synthesized, the film receives a $2.5 million equity investment for a feature production and $100,000 in screenplay development funding. Development and production are backed by Range Media Partners and Google's ‘100 Zeros’ initiative. Republic Film will open a public investment campaign for fans to invest in the feature.
It follows a boy who brings his deceased mother back through texts, her voice, and her diary. Once awakened, she never gives a single command. She only asks questions.

More than 2,500 entries came in from around the world, judged by Neil deGrasse Tyson, Neal Stephenson, Myra Lane and Rod Roddenberry. The four runners-up, ranked second through fifth, each receive $100,000 in cash. Second place went to Verena Puhm's ‘Nobody Dies on Mars,’ third to J. Ryan Williams's ‘Son Protocol,’ fourth to Aison Robbins's ‘Senti,’ and fifth to Hal Wattermuf's ‘Slingshot.’

‘The Gifted’ also topped the $100,000 ‘SPECS Audience Award,’ sponsored by Snap and decided entirely by public vote, winning $50,000. Voters watched pairs of films and chose which future they'd rather live in, and the 65 official selections were ranked using the Elo method. SandboxAQ supported the top 10 with $20,000 each.

Curious Refuge made this tutorial with AI animation instructor Albert Bozesan (@albertbozesan). It walks through, step by step, the latest AI workflow for merging 2D animation into live-action footage. It used Magnific's Seedance to generate video.

The starting point is the live-action edit. Since AI generation is expensive, they finish the edit, audio and basic color correction first, then export only the needed sections as 720p MP4s. Handheld shake is kept intact, since generated elements follow that movement to blend into the frame.

blocks.cap: Turnaround of the 2D beaver character

blocks.x: Next comes the reference. They made front, side and back turnarounds and an expression sheet for the 2D beaver, recommending an A-pose on a gray background instead of a T-pose. They were adamant that props like the whiskey bottle used in the shoot be used only as a shape reference.

Prompts were organized using Crumpet, a free tool Bozesan built himself. It lays out actions, like raising a finger, pulling out the bottle, pouring a drink, and holding out the glass, on a timeline to indicate the order. Instructions like maintaining the 2D style, cartoon motion and smear frames, and preserving the original camera shake are rewritten for each shot.

blocks.cap: The Crumpet timeline screen with actions laid out

blocks.x: The trickiest part was the cartoon fight between the cat and the beaver. Giving Seedance a tornado image as reference made it follow too literally, producing flat results. So they gave only character references and described the fight in text, controlling which chairs and paintings fell through the timeline. AI is good at chaos but struggles with restraint.

The remaining problems were solved with existing tools. The whiskey's color and blur were fixed in After Effects, and the missing glass was recomposited from a freeze frame. The conclusion: AI works best as part of a pipeline, not the whole thing.
The SF action film 'Steelray,' completed entirely with 100% AI technology, unveiled its poster and announced an October theatrical release.

'Steelray' (director Seol Woo-in; planning/production Raon Company Plus; co-production Inno Studio) follows a protagonist who tries to save humanity from a rampaging AI, fighting the worst virus with an AI he created himself and a battle suit left behind by his father.

The poster strikingly shows the protagonist Yoon Gang and the battle suit 'Steelray.' The autonomously-judging robot 'AIRA' deems humans a threat, and Yoon Gang, wearing the Steelray his father left him, faces a massive crisis alongside his own AI, 'Ara.' The tagline, “Now, shall we change the game?” heightens the tension before the final battle.

AI was not used in just a few scenes. It is a 'full-time AI production,' applying AI across the entire process from planning to production to post-production. It reduced the awkward movement and character expression common in AI video, and kept the visuals of scenes and characters consistent. Lip-sync was matched to actual voice actors' performances, and sound mixing was added as well.

The direction was handled by actor-director Seol Woo-in. He has appeared in 'It's Fairy Tale But R-Rated,' 'King the Land,' 'Oasis,' and 'Dr. Park Won-jang of Internal Medicine,' and first tried AI direction with 'Day One' in the AI omnibus 'Code G: The Start of Attention.'

Ha Jung-woo, standing vice chairperson of the National AI Strategy Committee, who watched the film in advance at a blind screening and insight talk, said, “I felt the need to much more actively address what's needed for Korea to lead globally as a cultural powerhouse in the AI era,” adding, “Through 'Steelray,' I confirmed that possibility.”
'Steelray,' which heralds the birth of a new K-hero, opens in theaters nationwide in October.

A French animators' group has demanded that the Annecy festival clearly state how it will use, display, and govern generative AI. The call comes as the festival finds itself at the center of the animation industry's AI debate.

blocks.cap: Annecy and generative AI

blocks.x: The standard they cite is the '3C' principle: compensation, control, and consent. Using creative work to train AI should require the creator's consent first, fair compensation for its use, and the creator's ability to control how their work is used.
The Annecy International Animation Film Festival runs from June 21 to 27. This year it put weight on creating a space where differing views on AI could meet.

blocks.cap: Mikaël Marin, Marcel Jean, Véronique Encrenaz

blocks.x: The centerpiece is the one-day think tank 'AI4Animation.' The discussions gathered there will form the basis of an animation AI white paper to be published in 2029. MIFA market director Véronique Encrenaz said she would compile the concerns and trends from the field.

This year's badge holders are expected to number about 18,400, similar to last year. The biggest change is the opening of the permanent venue 'Cité Internationale du Cinéma d'Animation,' which has a 332-seat theater, exhibition space, and workshop rooms.

Citia head Mikaël Marin said the festival should be a place where people clash and exchange views. Artistic director Marcel Jean said he would not rush to predict AI's impact on animators' jobs, and noted that schools are preparing students for the AI era.

blocks.cap: 'Gatto' (Pixar)

blocks.x: The competition lineup also includes works distributed by Canal+, such as Sébastien Laudenbach's 'Viva Carmen!' and Olivier Clert's 'Lucy Lost.' Marin said he was surprised by recent remarks from Canal+'s CEO, but that cooperation with major investors still has to be maintained.
Curious Refuge rounded up this week's AI film news in one place.

The biggest news is the Google-A24 partnership. Google is spending $75 million to jointly build AI production tools for professional studios. It's a sign Hollywood has moved from debating AI to actually using it.
Alibaba unveiled Happy Oyster 1.0, an experimental platform that instantly generates a scene when a viewer enters a prompt such as 'a bus arrives' or 'a dinosaur starts running.'

Seedance 2.0 4K creates native 4K video from the start instead of upscaling lower resolution, at a cost of about $1 per second. Seedance 2.5, coming in early July, adds 30-second generation, 50 reference images, and 3D model import.

Elsewhere, OpenArt's Vibe Directing builds a story bible and storyboard when you feed in a script, and Palmer helps with editing through natural language. CapCut's Create contest has put up a prize pool of more than $200,000.

Reallusion dropped the 30-day trial and released iClone Personal as a permanently free version. You can use the full 3D toolset, build scenes, create animation, and even render, all for free with no time limit.

blocks.cap: iClone Personal key visual

blocks.x: AI Studio has ended early access and launched as a full version. It strengthens character consistency and multi-reference support to keep an actor's likeness more accurate.

blocks.cap: AI Studio key visual

blocks.x: Licensing comes in three tiers. The free version offers unlimited creation and rendering, plus 30 exports for external 3D pipelines. A subscription removes the export limit, but reverts to the free tier if you stop subscribing. A perpetual license fully owns exports as well.

AI Studio's AI Actors (iModels) have been redesigned so a likeness doesn't break down even when the style changes, and they plug directly into the Seedance 2.0 video pipeline. You can bundle images, video, audio, AI Actors, and 3D scene data together. It supports Seedance 2.0, Kling 3.0, Veo 3, Nano Banana, and Flux.

blocks.cap: Character consistency maintained across camera cuts

blocks.x: The RTX render engine arrives as an open beta in late July, offered as a free update. AI Cloud plans are split into Starter, Standard, and Pro, and even free users get 500 AI points, 200 sample assets, and 12 starter AI Actors.

blocks.cap: AI Cloud plan breakdown

blocks.x: The 28th Shanghai International Film Festival closed on June 21. New directors, a foundation for nurturing creators, and AI's deep reach into production were the festival's three pillars this year.

blocks.cap: The 'Atlantic Rhapsody' team

blocks.x: Zhong Kaifeng's 'Atlantic Rhapsody' won Best Picture and Best Cinematography (Hao Zhaowei). In the Asian New Talent section, Gong Yiwen's 'Her First Taste' took Best Picture and Best Actress (Ma Pupu). Tony Leung chaired the jury.

AI ran through the program. Workshops covered image, audio, writing, and legal issues, and the festival partnered with generative AI company MiniMax. MiniMax vice president Yan Yijun said raising the picture quality of generative video models ultimately comes down to compute power.

One AI-focused company finished a 120-minute live-action period drama in seven days, using background replacement, relighting, VFX, and AI-generated actors. Panelists said generative AI assists rather than replaces human creativity, but unease in the audience did not go away.
Lisa Lu, an actress from 'Crazy Rich Asians,' received a lifetime achievement award. The opening ceremony featured a robotic arm performance and AI-generated video.

The 2026 Annecy International Animation Festival set a record with 19,100 badge holders, a sharp rise from 7,100 accredited attendees in 2013. France saw its hottest day on record on June 24, and artistic director Marcel Jean said some audiences skipped screenings to avoid the outdoor heat while waiting in line.

Many said this year's films were stronger than ever, but the industry faced upheaval not unlike live-action. Industrially, Annecy has become a stage as big as Cannes, in some ways bigger. 'Minions & Monsters,' the seventh installment of the top-grossing animated franchise 'Despicable Me/Minions,' opened the festival, and Disney/Pixar, Netflix, Warner Bros. Animation and others unveiled a wave of new titles.

This year's clearest trend was the rise of Asia, especially in animation. Netflix said viewing of its animated titles jumped from 1 billion views in 2023 to 1.5 billion in 2025. A preview of India's S.S. Rajamouli's 'Baahubali: The Eternal War' drew major buzz, and U.S. and European companies increasingly jumped into animation.
Oscar race talk was abundant too. Laika's 'Wildwood,' Netflix's 'Ray Gun' and DreamWorks' 'Forgotten Island' were among the titles mentioned as contenders, while shorts like 'God Is Shy' were cited.

But this year's most talked-about work was veteran animator Hisko Hulsing's short 'Dans Macabre.' Hulsing openly described using generative AI to mimic his own drawings, and audiences wearing 'Stop Generative AI' stickers gathered at the screening. Just before it began, some walked out and others booed. Marcel Jean countered, saying, 'I understand the concerns around AI, but I cannot agree with a witch hunt targeting an artist's work who is transparently exploring a new tool.'

Meanwhile, the market is fighting a crisis. Studios and major indies that were recruiting animators a decade ago have mostly disappeared, and students and newcomer animators carrying job-seeking signs wandered the MIFA market. The 'Cité du Cinéma d'Animation,' which opened on June 19, is an attempt to make Annecy animation's capital all year round.

A bill aimed at curbing unauthorized AI deepfakes passed the Senate Judiciary Committee. It marks meaningful progress on what the entertainment industry has called its top legislative priority this year.
The bill passed the committee unanimously by voice vote on Thursday. However, Republican Senators Mike Lee, Ted Cruz and Eric Schmitt raised concerns related to the First Amendment.
The bill is meant to address the spread of unauthorized 'deepfakes'; several actors have testified before Congress about cases where their voices and likenesses were stolen.

Under the bill, individuals hold the right to authorize digital replicas of their own voice and likeness. This digital replica right does not disappear after a person dies; heirs and executors can inherit it and grant permission for its use. However, posthumous rights are recognized for no more than 70 years after death.
News, documentaries and sports, as well as biographical works and uses for commentary, criticism or parody, are excluded from the bill's scope.

The bill has broad support from entertainment industry guilds and unions, studios and record labels, as well as tech companies such as OpenAI and Google/YouTube. An amendment released last month added a 'counter-notice' process for disputing takedowns and exemptions for certain work by libraries, archives and research institutions.
RIAA chairman and CEO Mitch Glazier said in a statement, 'We welcome today's passage by the Senate Judiciary Committee and look forward to it becoming law this year.'

At Thursday's markup, Cruz was especially concerned that 'satire, an important part of speech, needs to be protected.' He cited reality star Spencer Pratt, who recently used AI-generated images of Mayor Karen Bass and others in a biting ad during the Los Angeles mayoral race, saying Pratt's video was 'very funny, and a good example of something that should be protected, not caught by a law like this.' Pratt finished third in the mayoral primary and did not advance to the November runoff.

A companion bill with the same aim has been introduced in the House. Lawmakers who joined the push include Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), as well as Maria Salazar (R-Fla.) and Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.).
Another co-sponsor, Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), said, 'The rapid advance of generative AI has brought remarkable innovation, but it has also unleashed a wave of unauthorized exploitation.'

The White House has generally kept a hands-off approach to AI development, but in a national legislative framework released in March, the Trump administration signaled apparent support for policies similar to the NO FAKES Act.

Motion Picture Association (MPA) chairman and CEO Charles Rivkin said the bill 'establishes federal-level protections against malicious and deceptive use of digital replicas while respecting creators' constitutional rights and freedoms.' When a 2024 draft first appeared, studios warned that it could infringe on the First Amendment, but it was later revised to broadly exempt replicas that portray a person 'in a historical or biographical manner, including some degree of fictionalization.' Films like 'Forrest Gump' are seen as falling under this exemption.

The Human Artistry Campaign, an international coalition of artist and content creator organizations that also pushed for the bill's passage, said through senior advisor Moiya McTier, 'As AI evolves, everyone should have the right to control how their voice, likeness and identity are used.'

The issue has been especially important to voice actors, who have worried that unauthorized replication of their likenesses could threaten their livelihoods. National Association of Voice Actors (NAVA) president Tim Friedlander said, 'This passage is the result of a diverse, bipartisan coalition's efforts,' adding, 'Over the past two years, NAVA has taken part in more than 100 meetings on behalf of everyone who should have the right to their own voice, image, name and likeness.'
It remains unclear when, or whether, the bill will reach a full floor vote. Still, when it was first introduced in 2024, it did not even clear committee.

Cool is a slippery thing. The moment you think you've got a grip on it, it slips away like a water balloon. For the older generation, its embodiment was Martin Scorsese. A few weeks ago, when he got excited about signing a deal with an AI startup to use for storyboarding, the harder he tried to lend the company his legendary credibility, the more it only underscored the cool he no longer had.

For the younger generation, A24 has been cool for a while now. It probably still is, but Monday's puzzling partnership with Google DeepMind chipped away no small amount of that cool. Take $75 million from the world's biggest tech company under the banner of a slop tool, and you can't keep your countercultural credibility for long. That became clear the next day, when an entirely unrelated (non-AI) trailer for Jesse Eisenberg's community-theater movie got buried in mockery. "Why would I pay and root for a company that doesn't believe in or support the power of human creativity?" and "a24 was actually cool until you sold out to an AI giant for a few bucks of exclusivity money" were among the more polite comments.

It's easy to forget, but tech itself was once cool, back when Steve Jobs would make cinematic entrances at Apple's WWDC to show off the iPod and iPhone. It stayed that way through late 2022, when OpenAI released ChatGPT and everyone got excited turning Taylor Swift lyrics into Shakespearean sonnets. The vibe left the room after that moment. The shift from something fun you could hold in your hand to something intangible that billionaires use to control us is the core of this decline.

OpenAI, which enjoyed that last moment of cool, has now become the main force draining it. The fall became clear about a year after ChatGPT launched, when Sam Altman beat back an attempted ouster by safety-minded executives and board members with maneuvers that looked close to a backroom scheme. A year after that, the cool evaporated when Altman, along with Jeff Bezos, Tim Cook, Mark Zuckerberg, and Sundar Pichai, attended and donated to Donald Trump's inauguration. Anthropic has held out the longest, helped by Dario Amodei confronting Pete Hegseth head-on and Claude working far better than ChatGPT, but how long that lasts is anyone's guess.

Back to A24's standing. This company was supposed to stand against all of that. In an age of factory-made movies, it embraced Ari Aster, Greta Gerwig, Barry Jenkins, Ti West, and Josh Safdie, and in an age of sequels, it bet everything on Kane Pixels. Just a month ago, headlines weren't just saying A24 was cool; they were saying its cool outpaced Star Wars. Now that same company faces mockery and boycott threats. The power of Big Tech is that it can make something un-cool just as sharply as it once made it cool.

What's puzzling about the DeepMind deal isn't that A24 shouldn't have experimented with AI, it's that it ran the whole experiment wrong. It should have waited until it had something worth showing, released it, and silenced the skeptics, but instead it announced a corporate-to-corporate deal with nothing to show but 'trust us.' The anti-A24 mood will shift somewhat. It's nearly certain that a native generation of AI artists who express themselves through this technology will emerge before long. "Someone's going to make a terrifyingly great horror movie with this technology, and someone's going to make a genuinely funny comedy," said Matt Stone. Still, that doesn't help today's A24. Building cool takes years; giving it away takes just one awkward business move.
A24 and Google have formed an AI research partnership. The indie studio A24 is teaming up with Google's DeepMind division to develop new AI technology for filmmakers.

Google's investment tied to the partnership is about $75 million, roughly on par with what Thrive Capital put in during A24's previous funding round, according to the Wall Street Journal. The partnership gives A24 access to DeepMind's research and infrastructure, while DeepMind researchers help the studio design new workflows. The deal does not give Google access to A24's content library or data.

In an era when companies are bouncing between partnerships and lawsuits, this is another pairing between a Hollywood studio and AI. Disney signed a brief deal lending out its characters to OpenAI while suing AI companies like MiniMax and Midjourney for copyright infringement, and Lionsgate has expanded its collaboration with AI company Runway AI to develop new IP and pull in existing franchises to make AI-generated works. Netflix also acquired Ben Affleck's AI startup Int3ractive, which builds tools for filmmakers, earlier this year.

Scott Belsky, the partner leading the studio's technology division A24 Labs, told the Journal that the Google partnership is different from other deals, saying AI developers have wrongly marketed their products as a way to make movies cheaper and faster. His division is developing applications like AI-generated storyboards, another reimagining of the production process that filmmakers like Martin Scorsese have endorsed.

"We believe there are better uses that preserve creative control and support risk-taking," he told the Journal, adding that the new tools would be "nothing like the prompt-based generative AI that people are uncomfortable with."
"We believe breakthroughs happen when technology gets into the hands of the best minds in the field," said Eli Collins, vice president of product at DeepMind, in comments to the Journal.

A24 has been a haven for emerging filmmakers. Its critical and commercial success, from "Lady Bird" and "Moonlight" to "Everything Everywhere All at Once," "Marty Supreme," and the recent hit "The Backrooms," has come from the trust it placed in the filmmakers it works with and the passionate young fan base that trust built. (PostTrak data shows about 85% of the audience that saw "The Backrooms" in its opening week was under 35.) A Pew Research survey released last week found that about half of adults under 30 believe AI will harm society. This deal arrives against that backdrop.

blocks.x: 'Director,' which OpenArt will launch on Tuesday, is a tool from the Redwood City company led by two former Google engineers. Unlike most tools, which force users to painstakingly stitch together 5-to-10-second clips, Director lets you assemble a film up to five minutes long. It's a conversational system that starts at the storyboard stage and carries through to post-production, guiding users by the hand through completing a five-minute scene for a short or feature film.

Co-founder and CEO Coco Mao and her executives call this "vibe directing," borrowing the term vibe coding and bringing it into the writer's domain. "With vibe coding, you give it a vibe and you forget that there's even code," said Mao, who founded the company with former Google colleague John Chao. "You set direction, hand off the work, give feedback, and the machine figures it out. Vibe directing is similar: the user forgets about the tools or the technology and just has to imagine, react, and show their taste."

The company blends multiple models, from Seedance to Runway, to make films. Its strength lies in picking the model that best fits the situation, and, more decisively, in its simple interface. According to Mao, the goal is to "handle the small decisions for people so they aren't stuck writing prompts." Chief technology officer Amy Hur said that rather than training models, the company steered an agentic AI approach that uses goal-based rules to reach outcomes, which made a more intuitive interface possible.

In hands-on use, just a few sentences produced a script, and that script alone was enough to stitch together a film. But that's where the real work began. The first script was pretty rough, and it took far more revisions to get a usable result. Still, because it captured ideas with so little effort, it got the work started in a way a simple chatbot doesn't. It clearly lowers the barrier to filmmaking and draws in people who were intimidated by the process.

To promote Director, OpenArt is running pre-show theater ads, New York subway ads, and a billboard in West Hollywood. The company said its existing image and video tools have 8 million active subscribers. According to research firm Sacra, it has generated $70 million in revenue, and Mao said the company has about 50 employees. It recently raised about $30 million in funding, a fraction of the more than $800 million Runway has raised.

Gil Reef, a former head writer for The Ellen DeGeneres Show, said Director doesn't feel like being on set, but it "feels a lot like giving notes to an editor," adding that "with so much friction removed, it feels more creative than ever." Mao and Chao were previously known for Tangi, a short-video service from a Google incubator, before leaving in 2022 to start OpenArt. Mao said it's ushering in "a new era of storytelling" that will "create a lot of new storytellers, and give existing storytellers more freedom and expression."

blocks.cap: OpenArt Director's generation screen. The company believes the tool could usher in an era of 'vibe directing.'

blocks.x: After fans criticized A24 for embracing AI, the studio explained that its research partnership with Google DeepMind is an attempt to secure "a seat at the table" as Hollywood grapples with AI.

"This is a research collaboration," A24 publicist Sophia Shin said in a statement about the deal, first reported by Wired. "We are sitting alongside DeepMind researchers, learning, refining, building, and directly helping shape new tools and new ways of working."

The statement continued: "We don't take our relationship with audiences for granted. This partnership exists because we want to have a say in what tools get built for artists, and because we want artists to have a voice in shaping those tools rather than simply being handed them. We'd rather have a seat at the table than be pushed to the side."

Under the partnership, unveiled Monday by the studio and Google, A24 and its technology arm A24 Labs gain access to DeepMind's research and infrastructure, while DeepMind researchers work with the studio to design new ways of working and figure out what tools filmmakers might want. Google will not get access to A24's content library or data, however, and filmmakers won't be required to use the tools. A24 fans voiced their displeasure on social media, leaving comments on the studio's Instagram and X posts accusing it of betraying the audience that has supported it.

An Instagram post promoting the upcoming film 'The Debut' drew a comment reading, "What the hell is this AI collaboration? Do you even know your fanbase?" while an X user called the deal "disgusting."

Companies have been wrestling with how to engage with this ubiquitous technology while protecting copyright and intellectual property. Lionsgate expanded its partnership with AI company Runway this month, aiming to build new franchises from existing IP and produce AI-generated shows. DeepMind CEO and co-founder Demis Hassabis said in a blog post this week that "the best way to build tools that empower artists is to work directly with them."

He wrote that "partnering from the start with filmmakers and industry leaders like A24 lets us build new AI capabilities that help artists doing authentic, meaningful storytelling bring their creative vision to life."

'Backrooms' director Kane Parsons called generative AI "a symptom of broader cultural and economic decay" in an interview with The Australian earlier this month, saying that while it might have some use in VFX-related work, "there's too much at stake and too much real harm already happening to discuss it objectively."

He told the newspaper, "I think I'm in the same boat as most sane people. If I could snap my fingers and make generative AI disappear forever, I probably would. On the creative side, I get zero enjoyment from using that tool. For me, it completely undermines the purpose itself."
Adobe rolled out a bundle of Creative Cloud updates spanning Lightroom, Premiere, After Effects, Photoshop and Illustrator. New AI features now cover tasks ranging from culling photos to rotoscoping.

In Premiere, Global Audio Mute silences the entire app with a single click. Marker Search finds markers by color or name across every open project. Three new effects, Channel Blur, Gradient and Noise FX, handle compositing and moving-texture work right inside the timeline. The new 3D Spin Back and Slide transitions come with professional-grade easing controls. Single Word Captioning lets you edit caption text word by word without disturbing the surrounding caption block.

blocks.cap: Single Word Captioning in Premiere

blocks.x: Stock Panel Checkout lets you preview and license Adobe Stock assets without leaving Premiere. Bringing multiple assets into a project via Firefly Boards automatically builds out a sequence. Object Mask now has softer edges, and can regenerate after media goes offline and gets reconnected. The Sequence Index panel gathers long-form editing controls in one place, and the new A/V display mode shows video and audio waveforms together in the source monitor.

In After Effects, Object Matte replaces the brush-only Roto Brush, bringing four AI tools: Object Selection, Quick Selection, Selection Brush and Edge Refinement. The 3D toolset gains a displacement map for surface depth, depth of field across models, meshes, text and shape layers, and a scripting API for parametric meshes. SVG files can now be imported directly as editable shape layers that preserve gradients, strokes and transparency. Vector content can also be copied and pasted straight from Illustrator without conversion.

blocks.x: In Photoshop, Remove Reflections finds and removes reflections in glass, separating them onto their own layer so opacity can be adjusted non-destructively. The Remove tool now runs its generative AI model directly on-device, working both online and offline.

In Lightroom, Assisted Culling has moved out of early access to general release. The new feature adds Face View, which isolates people in a frame to analyze eye sharpness and whether their eyes are open. Stacking automatically groups near-identical images and flags the best candidate. Custom filters, precision dials and selection overrides allow finer control over the process.
Photo to Video turns still images into moving clips using AI-generated motion, powered by Firefly and Google Veo. You can use a prompt automatically pulled from the image or write your own.

AI Sharpen integrates Topaz Labs' noise-aware sharpening model directly into Lightroom with no separate export required. Sony a7R VI RAW files are now supported across Lightroom, Lightroom Classic and Adobe Camera Raw.

Illustrator's Concept to Vector, first introduced in Illustrator 30.5, turns sketches or low-resolution assets into editable vector drafts, or generates multiple style variations from a single source image.

The features arrive alongside Adobe's latest 2026 Creators Toolkit Report, which surveyed more than 16,000 creators across eight countries on how they view the creative software they use for their work. AI was at the center of the questions this year. 75% of creators said AI is integrated into or essential to their work, and 87% said AI has grown their business or audience. Exclusive: Tech-driven production company Asteria has formed a strategic partnership with video-generation model maker LTX. The goal is to advance cinematic AI storytelling.

The collaboration aims to close the technical gap between AI video and professional-grade production. LTX will now serve as the generative engine behind Asteria's AI-driven production, with results that can reach premium hybrid quality.
